text: Sazae-san is a Japanese yonkoma manga series created and illustrated by Machiko Hasegawa, first published in the local paper Fukunichi Shinbun on April 22, 1946. When the Asahi Shimbun offered Hasegawa to draw the four-panel comic for their paper, she moved to Tokyo in 1949, explaining that the main characters had relocated from Kyūshū to Tokyo. The first Sazae-san strip published by the Asahi Shimbun appeared on November 30, 1949, and the manga depicted everyday life and contemporary situations in Tokyo until Hasegawa retired, with the final comic released on February 21, 1974. The series dealt with the large family dynamic in a lighthearted, easy manner, and its final episode centered on Sazae's joy over a double yolk from an egg she cracked for her husband, with Katsuo commenting on the happiness found in small life moments. As of 1999, the manga had over 86 million copies in circulation, making it one of the best-selling manga series of all time, and it won the 8th Bungeishunjū Manga Award in 1962. An anime television adaptation by TCJ (later renamed Eiken) began airing in October 1969 and has remained on the air continuously, broadcasting every Sunday from 18:30 to 19:00 without change, featuring three vignettes. It holds the Guinness World Record for the longest-running animated television series, achieving the record on September 5, 2013, and as of December 2025, has aired over 9,000 episodes. The anime started as a slapstick comedy with references to Tom and Jerry and Looney Tunes but shifted to a family drama within a year, maintaining this style for over 50 years without major changes in directing, scriptwriting, or character design. The anime is considered a "national anime" in Japan with a 97% recognition rate in a 2020 NIPPON RESEARCH CENTER survey, and is seen as a symbol of universality and permanence. Despite its unchanging style, it is sometimes criticized as anachronistic due to the absence of smartphones and convenience stores, though the staff states they have no plans to update the setting to reflect modern elements. Elements like smoking and corporal punishment have been removed or addressed. The anime is not widely known outside Japan due to the rights holders' decision not to export or globally develop it, though the producer expressed hopes for future global expansion. Only Midori Katō, who voices Sazae, has never been replaced; she was recognized by Guinness World Records in 2019 for the longest career as a voice actor for the same animated character. Other main voice actors have changed: Ichirō Nagai, who played Namihei, was replaced in 2014 after his death at age 82, and Miyoko Asō, who voiced Fune, was replaced in 2015 to reflect her age at 89; Takako Sasuga, who voiced Tarao, died in 2023 at age 87 and was also replaced. Since 1974, the opening credits have introduced locations Sazae has visited in Japan, changing approximately every three months, and this has become a tourism promotion tool, with prefectures and municipalities providing 5–10 million yen in aid since 2000. From November 1991, each episode ends with a janken match between Sazae and viewers, replacing the earlier tradition of tossing a bean or rice cake in the air and catching it, which was changed due to health concerns raised by medical institutions. The anime was originally sponsored by Toshiba, which later expanded to other sponsors, though the association remained strong; when Toshiba withdrew due to poor management, it was widely reported. Sazae-san was the last animated TV series to use traditional cel animation, with the opening credits becoming digital in April 2009 and the series fully transitioning to digital animation in 2013. Hasegawa never wanted merchandise or home video rights for the series, and after her death, her request to keep older episodes from being released on home media was honored. However, in December 2018, Fuji TV partnered with Amazon Prime Video and other streaming services to release episodes from 1969 and the early-to-mid 1970s, along with some mid-2000s and mid-1990s to 2010s episodes. The opening and ending songs are original and sung by Yuko Uno, with the audio unchanged since the series began, though trimmed during early years. The series experienced two production suspensions: one for about a month in February 1975 due to the 1970s energy crisis, and another for about a month in May 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which past episodes were rebroadcast. In Japan, "Sazae-san syndrome" refers to a depressed mood on Sunday night after watching the show, signaling the end of the weekend. In 1955, a radio station aired a serial drama based on the comic, and a short-lived live-action TV series aired on what is now TBS. In November 1965, TBS launched a dramatic series modeled after the manga, which aired until September 1967. In 1979, NHK produced a six-month dramatic serial focusing on the creation of Sazae-san and Machiko Hasegawa. In 2010, Fuji Television launched a live-action situation comedy, Sazae-san 2, followed by Sazae-san 3 the next year, using the same elements including the theme music and closing janken match. In 2008, Glico featured the family in "25 years later" commercials for its "Otona Glico" chocolates, with actors Eita (Tarao), Tadanobu Asano (Katsuo), Rie Miyazawa (Wakame), and Shun Oguri (Ikura). In 2017, Sazae and Masao appeared in a Cup Noodles commercial drawn by Katsuya Kondō.
